through midnight Friday, though forecasters said the smoke may linger into early Saturday.</p><p>“Based on the latest forecast trends, it looks like air quality should gradually improve as that smoke pushes off to the northeast,” said Zachary Yack, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service. “The only caveat is it's a little unclear how fast things actually improve.”</p><p>Yack notes that as winds begin to push the smoke out of the area, it may linger near Lake Michigan before fully heading northeast.</p><p>The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency projects the air quality for Saturday to be moderate – the second least severe reading on the Air Quality Index scale.</p><p>While there is a chance smoke may return to the area Saturday afternoon, Yack says conditions won’t be as severe.</p><p>“It probably wouldn't be as intense as this last bout has been,” Yack said.</p><h3>Is this likely to happen every summer?</h3><p>Yes. This appears to be the new normal. In Chicago, we experienced similar conditions in 2023 when Canadian wildfires burned during a record year. Last year was also bad for Canadian fires; the city’s air <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2025/06/05/air-quality-alert-issued-throughout-chicago-area-due-to-canadian-wildfire-smoke" target="_blank" ><u>ranked among the worst in the world</u></a> in June of last year due to the smoke.</p><p>We’re seeing earlier and more intense forest fires in Canada as climate change is producing warmer spring temperatures and dryness up north</p><p>Ozone has also long been a problem during summer months. Ozone pollution, often called smog, forms when car, truck and factory emissions interact with sunlight. Chicago has never been in compliance with federal law requirements for protection from ozone air pollution.</p><h3>How can I protect myself?</h3><p>Limit your exposure outside, especially if you have a respiratory or other health condition. An N95 mask, like those commonly worn during the COVID pandemic, can protect against the dangerous particle pollution. Pregnant women, children, teenagers and older adults are also at higher risk.</p><p>“I think everyone should close their doors and windows to try to prevent the smoke from getting into their homes as much as possible,” said Dr. Jack Zhao, a pulmonary critical care doctor at Rush Copley Medical Center. “I equate being outside with a forest fire to smoking. entries.summary: <h3>Good morning, Chicago. ✶</h3><p>🔎 <b>Below</b>: For the first time since the pandemic, the city closed all beaches and outdoor swimming pools because of fumes from Canadian wildfires, which are becoming Chicago's new summertime normal.</p><p>🗞️ <b>Plus</b>: More details on what led up to the fatal shooting of a Chicago police officer, candidates allege machine politics are at play and more news you need to know. </p><p>📧 <b>Subscribe</b>: <a class="Link" href="https://newsletter-hub.suntimes.com/" target="_blank" ><i>Get our morning newsletter delivered to your inbox weekday mornings.</i></a></p><p>⏱️: <i>An 8-minute read</i></p><hr><p></p><h4> TODAY’S WEATHER 🌤️</h4><p>Partly sunny with scattered afternoon showers, a high near 91 and more widespread smoke. href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuyhdik-l-i/" target="_blank" >Canadian wildfire smoke prompts air quality alert for Chicago</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuyhdik-l-d/" target="_blank" >Brett Chase</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuyhdik-l-h/" target="_blank" >Mohammad Samra</a></h5><p><b>Hazy days of summer</b>: Smoke from more than 800 Canadian wildfires blew into Chicago on Thursday, polluting the air and making it dangerous to be outside for extended periods of time. The city's Air Quality Index ranged from very unhealthy to hazardous — the two most severe levels on the index.</p><p><b>Closed for safety</b>: For the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, the city closed its beaches and outdoor pools. The Chicago Park District canceled all outdoor activities that couldn’t be moved inside. Concerts, sports and other outdoor events <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuyhdik-l-k/" target="_blank" >were also canceled</a>.</p><p><b>How long will this last?</b>: A government air quality alert currently runs through midnight Friday. Experts say we can expect similar conditions to happen every summer, pointing to more intense forest fires in Canada as climate change produces warmer spring temperatures and dryness up north.</p><p><b>Protect yourself</b>: Experts encourage limiting time outside, especially if you have a respiratory or other health condition. N95 masks can protect against dangerous particle pollution, and they can be found in a number of locations, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuyhdik-l-u/" target="_blank" >including hardware stores</a>.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuyhdik-l-o/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>POLICING 🚨</h4><div failed to place troubled cop under strict supervision before he fatally shot partner</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuyhdik-l-p/" target="_blank" >Peter Nickeas</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuyhdik-l-x/" target="_blank" >Casey Toner</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wuyhdik-l-m/" target="_blank" >Tom Schuba</a></h5><p><b>New details</b>: Chicago Police Officer Carlos Baker was referred to a program for troubled cops just weeks before he fatally shot his partner, Krystal Rivera, records show. Once in the Chicago Police Department's Personnel Concerns Program, Baker could have been placed under strict supervision or even been fired if he didn’t improve. entries.title: Man dies after being pulled from Lake Michigan near Playpen
entries.summary: <p>A man died after he was pulled from Lake Michigan Thursday afternoon in Streeterville near the Play Pen. </p><p>Chicago police marine unit personnel responded to the 800 block of North Lake Shore Drive for a person in the water and pulled 39-year-old Justin Kramarczyk from the lake, police and the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>Kramarczyk, of the Near South Side, was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital initially in critical condition but was pronounced dead at 3:39 p.m., the medical examiner's office said. </p><p>Tucked in an enclave between Oak Street and Ohio Street beaches, the Playpen is a popular party spot for boaters on summer weekends in Chicago. The location has experienced its share of high-profile rescues and drownings in recent years.</p><p>In July of 2023, a woman was killed and six people were rescued when a boat <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/7/28/23810986/six-rescued-boat-distress-call-in-lake-off-oak-street-beach" target="_blank" >hit a breakwall</a> near the Playpen. In August 2022, a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2022/8/16/23308250/playpen-boat-accident-lana-batochir" target="_blank" >woman’s feet were severed</a> in a boating accident.</p><p>A week after that incident a man’s body was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/8/20/23314729/spencer-william-body-playpen-lake-michigan" target="_blank" >pulled from the lake</a> in the Playpen area.</p><p>No further information was immediately available. <br></p>

entries.title: Is Frank Gehry's Icehenge desk headed to a museum?
entries.summary: <p>The 7-ton glass desk designed by the late architect Frank Gehry might end up in a museum — at least in the short term — the auction house that oversaw the item's sale said Friday.</p><p>Called Icehenge, the 16-piece emerald glass desk created for the lobby of the Inland Steel Building sold Wednesday for $243,200.</p><p>"The buyer is dedicated to maintaining public access to Icehenge and is considering a temporary loan to a suitable museum or institution," a representative of the Chicago office of Freeman's said. "Currently, no specific plans have been finalized."</p><p>So who's the successful bidder? Freeman's wouldn't say.</p><p>But Icehenge's new owners are not Gehry friends Thomas and Margot Pritzker, or their foundation, a Pritzker spokesperson told me.</p><p>It was worth asking: Gehry was awarded the Pritzker Architecture Prize in 1989.</p><p>Internationally-known architect Adrian Smith also didn't wind up with the desk. His firm, Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, is located in the Inland Steel Building, 30 W. Monroe St.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c40000" name="image-c40000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fbb72e1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7384x4144+0+390/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F7e%2F18377e5d46638574b17545e13ce8%2Fgehry-260707-07.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/813d510/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7384x4144+0+390/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F7e%2F18377e5d46638574b17545e13ce8%2Fgehry-260707-07.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b73206a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7384x4144+0+390/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F87%2F7e%2F18377e5d46638574b17545e13ce8%2Fgehry-260707-07.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Exterior of the Inland Steel Building at 30 W. Monroe St.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The auction result is an interesting addendum to a small but noteworthy chapter in Chicago’s storied history of architecture and design.</p><p>Working with John Lewis Glass Studio, now <a class="Link" href="https://www.christisonlewis.com/about" target="_blank" >Christison Lewis</a>, in Oakland, California, Gehry created the 15,000-pound desk unit specifically for the Inland Steel lobby.</p><p>The work — a staffed and functioning security desk — was installed in the building in 2012.</p><p>Gehry <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2025/12/06/architect-frank-gehry-obituary-millennium-park-music-pavilion-foot-bridge-dies-96" >died in 2025</a> at age 96.</p><p>Icehenge is as much sculpture as it is furniture, with the same billowing, sail-like quality found in many of Gehry's designs. But the work is also visually untamed, jagged and unpredictable.</p><p>"It does look like an explosion in a glass factory, kind of," the Los Angeles architect told Chicago architecture critic Blair Kamin in 2013. "If you actually had an explosion at a glass factory, apart from everyone getting killed, it would be pretty exciting visually."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: Amazon recibe las primeras aprobaciones municipales para un centro de distribución en Gage Park
entries.summary: <p>Los planes de Amazon para su más reciente centro de distribución de entrega local —el cuarto en Chicago— avanzaron significativamente el jueves.</p><p>La Comisión del Plan de Chicago otorgó la primera aprobación municipal para el centro de entrega local de Amazon de 235,137 pies cuadrados en la antigua planta de Central Steel & Wire, ubicada en la cuadra 3000 al oeste de 51st St. Amazon adquirió el sitio en 2021 por $35 millones —uno de sus <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2021/7/14/22577872/amazon-buys-sw-side-property-for-35-million" target="_blank" >mayores acuerdos de terrenos</a> en Chicago en ese momento.</p><p>Los centros de entrega local de Amazon son la parada final del proceso de entrega antes de que los paquetes lleguen a las puertas de los clientes. También tiene otros tres centros de entrega local en la ciudad, incluido uno en Bridgeport que se inauguró en julio de 2025. En ese momento, la instalación de Bridgeport empleaba a unas 150 personas.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b00000" name="module-b00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Amazon tiene cuatro sitios de operaciones,en Bridgeport, Back of the Yards, Pullman y West Humboldt Park, según la compañía. También cuenta con un centro de distribución en <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2021/4/7/22372242/amazon-online-retailer-working-conditions-protest-walkout-gage-park-facility" target="_blank" >Gage Park</a>.</p><p>La nueva instalación ofrecerá a los residentes de Gage Park “entregas más rápidas, mejores y más eficientes”, dijo Kyle DeGuilio, gerente principal de políticas de desarrollo económico para Amazon.</p><p>El equipo de desarrollo enfatizó que la instalación ocupará tres acres del sitio de aproximadamente 69 acres, con “amplios espacios”. La instalación medirá por lo menos lo de un campo de fútbol americano, o 360 pies, de las calles colindantes. La línea Naranja de la Autoridad de Tránsito de Chicago (CTA) está al norte de la propiedad.</p><p>“Estamos tomando una propiedad que ha sido completamente industrial desde finales de los años 30 y reemplazándola con una instalación de bajo perfil, con un amplio jardín que se centra en el espacio abierto”, dijo Jeff Cali, vicepresidente principal de servicios de desarrollo en Venture One Real Estate. Venture One está desarrollando la propiedad en representación de Amazon.</p><p>También en el sitio habrá 244 espacios de estacionamiento y un edificio de servicio de flota de 4,500 pies cuadrados con tres muelles de carga. El equipo de construcción indicó que la mayoría de los vehículos, incluidos los camiones de entrega, llegarán y saldrán fuera de las horas pico para reducir el impacto del tráfico en los vecinos.</p><p>La seguridad del tráfico y de los peatones fueron dos de las principales preocupaciones de los vecinos con respecto a la instalación propuesta, según la concejal Jeylú Gutiérrez (14.°).</p><p>Amazon planea realizar “un paisajismo significativo” en el sitio, que incluirá árboles alrededor del perímetro del lote para dividirlo de los vecinos, según su presentación a la comisión. Dos acres en la esquina sureste del sitio también serán donados al Distrito de Parques de Chicago para mantenerlos como espacio abierto, destacó Cali. La oficina de Gutiérrez mencionó que Amazon se ha comprometido a financiar el desarrollo del espacio del parque.</p><p>“En los últimos meses, he estado en comunicación regular con Amazon. Aprecio su disposición para escuchar, involucrarse y reconocer que están llegando a una comunidad que históricamente ha sido subatendida y demasiado a menudo pasada por alto para la inversión”, escribió Gutiérrez en una carta de apoyo al proyecto. “Espero continuar trabajando con Amazon para asegurar que esta inversión beneficie tanto a los residentes del 14.° distrito como a la compañía en los años venideros”.</p><p>Si se aprueba, Amazon espera comenzar la construcción en octubre, con una finalización en septiembre de 2027.</p><p>El desarrollo generaría aproximadamente 350 empleos temporales en la construcción. Una vez en operación, Amazon dijo que empleará a unos 200 empleados. Los sueldos por hora empezarán en $21.50, con beneficios incluidos. Se agregarán 400 empleos adicionales para socios de servicio de entrega.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Sky push practice facility opening to November, will not move in this season
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> have another new timeline for completion of their practice facility in Bedford Park: this time it's November.</p><p>That means they will not move in this season, as co-owner Nadia Rawlinson and CEO Adam Fox previously said they would. Instead, the Sky will practice at Wintrust Arena for the remainder of the season.</p><p>“It’s disappointing,” center Elizabeth Williams, who is also secretary of the players’ union, told the Sun-Times. “I think on their end it is as well because they had expectations for us and brought us in with those expectations as well. On their end, not being able to get that done sucks.”</p><p>Point guard Courtney Vandersloot echoed that sentiment last week.</p><p>“We’re all frustrated that it isn’t on time,” she said. “That’s from the very top all the way down. We wish we were in there. But I know that they’re doing it the right way, and it’s going to be a perfect home for us.”</p><p>Players were informed Thursday that they would not move into the facility this season, and general manager Jeff Pagliocca broke the news to reporters Friday. He cited construction challenges, including supply-chain and material delays. The project previously was delayed by weather and an expansion of the plans.</p><p>Pagliocca said the facility could be operational before the season ends, but the team decided it did not make sense to move into the building while construction was still ongoing.</p><p>“It mattered a lot to me that we gave the experience Day 1, not just components of it,” Pagliocca said. “When the wow factor hits, we want it to hit.”</p><p>The expectation now is that the facility will be available for offseason workouts — an important window for players who remain in-market and for the next free-agency cycle.</p><p>But each missed timeline makes the next one harder to believe. The delays hurt the Sky’s reputation around the league and erode trust with their own players.</p><p>Veteran point guard Skylar Diggins expressed frustration last week that the team did not have everything it needed to be successful.</p><p>“I was thinking we were going to be in a practice facility, and other things that were told to me,” she said. “And that’s not been the case. There’s been things outside of people’s control that I understand, too, a lot of moving parts. Lots of places I’ve been were in that process as well, so I get it. But it’s hard to perform at a certain level without those [resources].”</p><p>The Sky began the season practicing at UIC, then moved to Loyola before shifting practices to their home arena.</p><p>Williams said there are at least some advantages to practicing where the Sky play their home games. Wintrust Arena also has a number of recovery resources available, including hot and cold tubs, a training room and a weight room.</p><p>Still, it’s another missed timeline for a facility players were told they would use this season.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a entries.title: Como en la pandemia y dada la contaminación por incendios, las mascarillas son nuevamente imprescindibles
entries.summary: <p>Los habitantes de Chicago se apresuraron a ir a las tiendas el jueves para conseguir lo que necesitaban para proteger sus pulmones frente a los <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/16/wildfire-smoke-prompts-air-quality-alert-for-most-of-chicago-area-to" target="_blank" >niveles peligrosos de contaminación causados por el humo de incendios forestales canadienses</a>.</p><p>Elizabeth Keough, asistente de gerencia en el Crafty Beaver Home Center en el vecindario de Uptown, dijo que la afluencia de clientes el jueves fue mucho mayor de lo esperado, dada la dura situación afuera.</p><p>“Estamos vendiendo muchos filtros de aire y también nos estamos quedando sin mascarillas”, destacó Keough. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ab0000" name="module-ab0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Jin Kim, copropietario de Kim’s Hardware, afirmó que también observó un “aumento masivo”.</p><p>La semana pasada pidió 200 mascarillas KN95 más económicas, aunque menos efectivas, sin haber visto las noticias sobre los incendios forestales. Aun así, los paquetes individuales de mascarillas N95 más caras, equipadas con válvulas, eran el artículo más codiciado, lo que lo llevó a hacer más pedidos.</p><p>“Desde el COVID, cuando las ferreterías eran las únicas tiendas abiertas, éramos los únicos que teníamos mascarillas”,señaló Kim. “A nosotros nos funcionó… Tengo planeado comprar más, ya hemos agotado parte del inventario que entries.title: Air quality alert for Chicago, Day 2, as wildfire smoke from Canada shuts down beaches, venues
entries.summary: <p>Thick, acrid smoke still blanketed the Chicago area Friday, prompting closings and cancellations in the city and suburbs. </p><p>An air quality alert is in effect through midnight Friday, though forecasters said the smoke could linger into early Saturday. </p><p>Chicago's Air Quality Index hovered around "hazardous" by 10:30 a.m. Friday — the most severe level for airborne pollutants. </p><p>“It looks like air quality should gradually improve as that smoke pushes off to the northeast,” said Zachary Yack, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service. “The only caveat is it's a little unclear how fast things actually improve.”</p><p>Citing the air quality, all Chicago beaches and outdoor pools were closed until further notice, the Chicago Park District said. The Osaka Garden, the Garfield Park Conservatory and the Lincoln Park Conservatory also are closed for the day, while all outdoor park district programs were moved indoors. The Chicago Architecture Center was among other attractions also closed for the day.</p><p>Beaches in Evanston were closed for the day, and all non-urgent, non-public-safety-related outdoor work activities were paused, including recycling collections in the north suburb. Evanston summer camps were moved indoors, and all camps that couldn’t be relocated were canceled. The Morton Arboretum in Lisle also was closed to the public.</p><p>Organizers for some events in the area were waiting to make final decisions about whether to cancel. The Ravinia Festival in Highland Park, which launched its outdoor concert series last weekend with a $70 million renovation, was "closely monitoring air quality" in advance of tonight's scheduled 8 p.m. Paul Simon performance. </p><p>Ravinia planned to go ahead with Friday's Steans Institute Chamber Music concert, scheduled for 1:30 p.m. inside Bennett Gordon Hall, closing it to the public but making the show <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/raviniafestival" target="_blank" >available to stream on Ravinia’s YouTube channel</a>.</p><p>The Lakeview Roscoe Village Chamber of Commerce said it was "closely monitoring" air quality ahead of the Roscoe Village Burger Fest, which was scheduled to kick off at 5 p.m.</p><p>Yack said that, as winds begin to push the smoke out of the area, it still could linger near Lake Michigan before fully heading northeast.</p><p>The Illinois Environmental Protection Agency projects that air quality Saturday will be moderate — the second-least severe reading on the Air Quality Index scale.</p><p>While there is a chance smoke could return Saturday afternoon, Yack said conditions won’t be as severe.</p><p>“It probably wouldn't be as intense as this last bout has been,” Yack said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/16/wildfire-smoke-prompts-air-quality-alert-for-most-of-chicago-area-to" >‘Hazardous’ Canadian wildfire smoke prompts air quality warning for Chicago. Here’s what you should know.</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/16/air-quality-outdoor-events-canceled-list-concerts-beaches" >These events are canceled in the Chicago area due to Canadian wildfire smoke</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p><i>Contributing: Cassie Walker Burke</i></p>

entries.title: Chicago murals: Graffiti artists reunite decades later to tag Evanston wall
entries.summary: <p>Four friends who grew up graffitiing Evanston walls returned to their hometown this month to add more color and to celebrate the addition of a new “permission wall” for the next generation of writers.</p><p>Garrett Munski, Ole Flores, Alex Mendoza and Jordan Nickel grew up tagging walls, viaducts, underpasses and more as kids in Evanston in the 1990s and early 2000s. Nickel built his adult career around creating art, working under the artist name POSE, Munski went on to work as a mechanic while Flores is a CPA. Mendoza owns his own sign company.</p><p>The four reunited for the first time in decades earlier this month, when they gathered to legally tag a wall on Green Bay Road at Simpson Street. Johnny Cash and Buena Vista Social Club blasted while the four created their individual panels with color and spray cans.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" entries.title: MLB restricts dugout iPads to bar use of AI to make game decisions
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — Major League Baseball is restricting iPad usage in dugouts to prevent the tablets from running artificial intelligence to help make decisions.</p><p>The tablets have access to video and league-provided data, and also included a custom tab where teams could access other programs. MLB made the custom tabs inaccessible to teams starting Wednesday night.</p><p>"In many cases, the custom tab had expanded the use of the dugout iPads beyond their originally intended purpose to include recommendations regarding substitutions, pitch calling, and other in-game decisions traditionally made by players and coaches," MLB executive vice president of baseball operations Morgan Sword wrote in a June 11 memo to general managers, assistant GMs and video coordinators.</p><p>The memo, first reported by The Athletic, was obtained by The Associated Press.</p><p>A review by the competition committee found clubs had been compliant with the regulations.</p><p>"Instituting this prohibition beginning with the second half of the season is intended to provide clubs that have relied on the custom tab with appropriate lead-time to make any necessary adjustments," Sword wrote.</p><p>MLB started a pilot program allowing use of iPads in dugouts with restrictions late in the 2015 season and expanded their use in 2016 under a deal with Apple. Video was eliminated in the 2020 COVID season following the Houston Astros' sign-stealing scandal, then returned in 2021.<br></p>

entries.summary: <p>The better team vs. the privileged, preferred, chosen one.</p><p>The No. 2 FIFA ranked team in the world vs. the world No. 1 team and the World Cup defending champs.</p><p>The confirmed future of the sport vs. the sport’s confirmed G.O.A.T. The two will face each other in the 2026 World Cup final. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Joan Monfort/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Spain vs. Argentina. Argentina vs. the World.</p><p>The narrative choices as we sit on the promontory of this World Cup final tell a story of a five-week event that, on paper, lived beyond its own lofty expectations while, off-purpose, delivered a 103-game exposé on everything wrong and corrupt about the game of soccer on the world stage when FIFA gets involved.</p><p>Yet the Europe vs. South America installment of what will take course over the 90-plus-extra time minutes damn-near erases all of the neoliberalism vs. geopolitical dictatorship that makes the World Cup so ugly, breathtaking and addictive at the same time.</p><p>It’s often hard to appreciate a global championship when the sport itself — or the sport’s governing body — gets in front of the game. Spain’s masterclass against France further proved (by shutting them out, making it six shutouts in seven matches so far this World Cup and only allowing one goal in the 2-1 victory over Belgium) that defense gets countries to championships. And Argentina’s inability to lose and finally win a game on their own merits (without perceived and believed assistance from the referees, VAR, FIFA or England coach Thomas Tuchel's mysterious tactical adjustments), can erase all of the conspiracies.</p><p>Even in a World Cup when the world is watching, dissecting and internalizing e-v-e-r-y-thing. </p><p>Regardless of the galvanizing “no sport compares to futbol” energy that has come from this World Cup, in spite of the brilliancy and intensity of competition and play that’s been on display, despite the fact there being in this WC alone 37 goals scored in stoppage time (after the 90th minute) allowing it to be deemed one of the most dramatic World Cups ever, dissension persists. With Argentina being the reason for so much of the Cup’s contentions.</p><p>The hundreds (maybe thousands-on-thousands) of video posts deep-diving into favoritism throughout this entire World Cup given to Argentina and Lionel Messi to assure them a “proper” repeat of not just an appearance in the Final but a repeat of the crown, despite Messi’s “nothing was handed to us” comments, tells a story. One which came at the total cost of exposing the full-on racial and discriminatory and imperialistic history of Argentina. Including an Argentine player, Gianluca Prestianni, (who was not a part of their World Cup roster) being the one responsible for the implementation of the “Vini Jr. Law” into the sport, and social media influencer Darren Watkins Jr. (aka: IShowSpeed) while live streaming during the Argentina/Cape Verde match, as he was wearing Cape Verde kit, after the loss, being told by Argentinians/La Albiceleste fans to ”go cry at the zoo.”</p><p>And how Messi has been silent (same neutrality as another G.O.A.T. has been accused of) during all of it while his name and mastery on the pitch will after this World Cup forever be unseparated.</p><p>How this World Cup, more than any in the past, put on display the extent and effect of global colonialism, ethnic bigotry, coerced migration, transatlantic slavery, favored corruption stemming from all things, like, the blatant disregard towards Egypt’s coach both during and after his teams match against Argentina, Senegal’s “assisted” and “cruel” loss to Belgium, a Paraguayan government official calling next G.O.A.T. Kylian Mbappe a “colonized Cameroonian pretending to be French,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/soccer/2026/07/06/trump-fifa-actions-around-folarin-balogun-suspension-puts-world-cup-integrity-in-question" >the Trump “phone call”</a> to FIFA president Gianni Infantino that became one of the most emboldened and unhidden acts of circumvented intercontinental favoritism and cronyism ever exhibited during a professional sporting event.</p><div real with it) World Cup finale sports’ version of everything: It was evident in the bilateralism of the first semifinal between France and Spain, and even more evident in the historic dislike (hatred?) between England and Argentina in the other semi that led to this World Cup’s conclusion. Bringing to the pitch that fact that in the 1500’s Juan Diaz de Solias established a colony that would become Buenos Aires with Spain eventually integrating Argentina into their empire a few centuries later.</p><p>(Also Messi’s own personal history with Spain, as he moved from Rosario in Argentina to Barcelona, Spain, at age 13, to only choose to play for his birth country over his adopted one as a professional.)</p><p>Expect yellow cards-a-poppin’; a level of physicality from the opening kick to set the agenda of a match that corny white announcers will call “chippy;” breathtaking 1-on-1 battles; prepare for the unforgettable.</p><p>Just know as you watch what FIFA allowed to happen during this tournament to allow it to get to this ending. To totally separate this Spain/Argentina “War of Independence” from all that happened to get it here would be thoughtless. Because what FIFA did was answer a lot of questions about who the were, are and will continue to be. Even at the expense of the beauteousness of the game.<br></p>

entries.title: What to know about diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>Illinois has confirmed 309 cases of the diarrhea-causing illness cyclosporiasis, the state’s public health department confirmed Friday.</p><p>Cyclosporiasis is not considered deadly and is more of an inconvenience that in rare cases could have complications, said Dr. Emily Landon, an infectious diseases specialist at University of Chicago Medicine. In Illinois, 24 people have been hospitalized, according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. Most of the people in Illinois who have contracted the illness had traveled recently — 125 people internationally and 152<b> </b>domestically. It’s unclear if the other 32 traveled.</p><p>Higher numbers of cyclosporiasis are typically reported in the summer, but this year has seen an especially high number, health officials said.</p><p>The increase in Illinois is part of a larger number of cases in most states. Across 34 states, 1,645 cases have been reported, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.</p><p>Here's what you need to know about cyclosporiasis in Illinois.</p><h3><b>What is cyclosporiasis?</b></h3><p>Pronounced sigh-klo-spore-EYE-uh-sis, cyclosporiasis is an intestinal illness caused by the microscopic parasite cyclospora. Infection often comes after eating fresh fruits and vegetables and can lead to watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, gas and nausea.</p><p>The heat-loving parasite infects the bowels and spreads through feces. In the past, people have been infected by consuming fruits or vegetables that were exposed to feces-contaminated irrigation water. </p><h3><b>What is causing cyclosporiasis in Illinois?</b></h3><p>No definitive source has been identified for the current outbreak in Illinois, but past outbreaks have been linked to imported fresh produce, like bagged salad kits and berries, according to the state health department.</p><p>Cyclosporiasis is not transmitted from person to person, Landon said. Even if a person becomes sick, people don’t usually contaminate objects in their house enough to spread it to someone else.</p><h3><b>How long does it take to recover?</b></h3><p>People should talk to their doctor about getting tested if they have symptoms, so health officials can continue to track the outbreak, said Gwen Biggerstaff, the CDC’s deputy director of foodborne, waterborne and environmental diseases.</p><p>Most people who contract the illness recover in one to two weeks, according to the CDC. Many can recover with rest and plenty of fluids, but some may need antibiotics.</p><p>People can experience bloating, gas and dehydration but rarely have more complications.</p><p>“The problem with this disease is it can be kind of persistent,” Landon said. “And you can feel pretty sick, and then you can be starting to get better, and then the diarrhea can come back again.” </p><h3><b>Should I stop eating fresh fruits and vegetables? </b></h3><p>If a person is immunocompromised or has an underlying medical condition, they should take more precautions, Landon said. That’s especially true, for example, for those undergoing surgery soon or cancer treatments.</p><p>Everyone can follow typical food safety guidelines like washing hands and thoroughly washing and scrubbing fresh produce. Illinois health officials also suggest:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-b5494250-808c-11f1-a776-3b92d1e3bbf6"><li>Incorporating more fruits and vegetables with peels or outer layers</li><li>Eating canned fruits and vegetables</li><li>Keeping produce separate from raw meat and seafood</li><li>Refrigerating cut, peeled, or cooked fruits and vegetables within two hours</li><li>Refrigerating perishable produce.</li><li>Cooking vegetables to at least 158 degrees Fahrenheit </li></ul><h3><b>Is it safer to buy produce from my local Illinois farmers market? </b></h3><p>Fruits and vegetables coming from a smaller, local producer are likely to have less of a risk for contamination than food from massive manufacturers, Landon said. That’s especially true if an outbreak is centered on a certain product, but officials this time around don’t know if that’s the case.</p><p>So you shouldn’t assume there’s zero risk in buying from a local vendor because any farm can become contaminated, especially because of the current weather, Landon said.</p><p>Vendors at Chicago farmers markets haven’t seen a decline in sales so far, but they have gotten more questions from customers.</p><p>“We are quite confident that it is not coming from our farm or any of the other local family farms around us,” said Christina Gelder of Ellis Family Farms. She added that they are in close contact with Michigan State University to track research related to the cyclosporiasis outbreak.</p><p>Chelsa Moore shopped for produce at the Pullman Farmers Market after going down a “rabbit hole” searching for best practices to avoid getting sick. She’s avoiding prepackaged food and triple rinsing produce at home.</p><p>“I’m kind of leaning toward the side of just like not buying anything from the big stores and going to the local farmers market,” she said. “And then even doing even more with prepping and cleaning.” </p><h3><b>How is Illinois tracking the cases?</b></h3><p>The Illinois Department of Public Health is working with local health officials to collect data on the cases. They are also working with the CDC to investigate a potential source of the illness.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/cyclosporiasis/outbreaks/07-26/index.html" target="_blank" >CDC</a> has identified shredded lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Michigan, Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia as a source of widespread outbreaks in those states. Michigan has reported 4,312 cases as of Friday, which is more than the total national figure the CDC has reported. Taylor Farms supplied lettuce to Taco Bell, The New York Times reported.</p><p>In a statement, Taco Bell announced it was removing the affected lettuce from its supply chain across the country and planned to replace it in select states.</p><p>Several states — including Illinois — have reported cases unrelated to that cluster, said Biggerstaff, of the CDC. The federal agency also is investigating other outbreaks that could be connected.</p><p>The Chicago Department of Public Health as of Friday had not identified the source of local cases. One individual had eaten at Taco Bell but had also traveled to one of the states that is part of the larger outbreak. The department is seeing an increase in cases among Latinos who had not recently traveled internationally.</p><p>The number of cases locally and across the country could be higher, Landon said. That’s because testing for cyclosporiasis is expensive, and some insurance may not cover it. But as cases of cyclosporiasis are more in the news, doctors will likely start testing more patients or prescribe antibiotics to treat it if someone has symptoms.</p><p>If a person is confirmed to have cyclosporiasis, Landon said it’s important to cooperate with the local health department to detail everything they ate so officials can pinpoint the outbreak source.</p><h3><b>Are federal cuts affecting the outbreak? </b></h3><p>Last summer, the federal government scaled back a program known as the Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network that monitored foodborne illnesses, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/health/health-news/cdc-quietly-scaled-back-surveillance-program-foodborne-illnesses-rcna227089?link_source=ta_bluesky_link&taid=68add0b9b2316600014ce6de&utm_campaign=trueanthem&utm_medium=social&utm_source=bluesky" target="_blank" ><u>NBC News previously reported</u></a>. As part of the changes, reporting for cyclospora parasites became optional in 2025, according to the program’s website. The government had previously collected that data since 1997.</p><p>The scaled-back federal program worked with the FDA to proactively test certain foods to check if recalls were necessary, Landon said.</p><p>It’s hard to assess how much changes on the federal level are playing a role in the current outbreaks, Landon said. But it’s something health officials across the country should consider.</p><p>“It’s a combination of the nature of the illness, the fact that it’s happening at a time when there’s other sporadic cases, and then the lack of infrastructure and resources available for testing does matter,” Landon said, summing up the factors driving the outbreak. <br></p>

entries.title: Review: Rush, featuring explosive drummer Anika Nilles, turns reunion tour into joyful celebration of life
entries.summary: <p>On the first of four sold-out nights at Chicago’s United Center, Anika Nilles arrived poised to upend the expectations of one of rock’s most famously male-dominated audiences. Steadfast Rush fans proved to be absolutely ready for it.</p><p>The veteran Canadian progressive rock trio had ceased activity following its R40 tour in 2015. The shutdown was largely attributed to drummer and lyricist Neil Peart’s wishes to retire after decades of wear due to the punishing physicality of his playing and to spend time with his young family. Peart was acclaimed among rock’s premier drummers by audiences and musicians alike.</p><p>Unfortunately, a glioblastoma cut short his opportunity to enjoy an idyllic home life. Peart died in 2020 at age 67. Afterward, bassist and singer Geddy Lee and guitarist Alex Lifeson publicly stated that the loss of their crucial bandmate and friend meant the end of Rush.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: Junta de Elecciones recomienda que candidatos independientes no aparezcan en la boleta para el puesto de García
entries.summary: <p>Los oficiales de audiencia de la Junta de Elecciones del Estado de Illinois están recomendando que los candidatos independientes del 4.º Distrito Electoral, el concejal Byron Sigcho-López y Mayra Macías, no aparezcan en la boleta de noviembre por no haber presentado el número mínimo de firmas válidas de las peticiones, una queja que ambos atribuyen directamente a la política de la maquinaria demócrata.</p><p>Una decisión oficial se tomará el martes cuando se reúna la Junta de Elecciones del Estado de Illinois para emitir un fallo, y la junta es libre de desviarse de la recomendación. Sin embargo, el oficial de audiencia Joseph A. Craven escribió en un documento publicado el jueves que Macías estaba a sólo 486 firmas de alcanzar el requisito mínimo de 10,816 firmas para postularse como candidata independiente. Escribió que “no puede recuperar la validez de las firmas suficientes”.</p><p>La oficial de audiencia, Barbara Goodman, escribió que Sigcho-López tampoco debería figurar en la boleta de noviembre por no alcanzar el número de firmas requerido.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b60000" name="module-b60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Goodman señaló que el abogado de Sigcho-López, Andrew Finko, planteó argumentos constitucionales y "preocupaciones por lo que él caracterizó como una conducta opresiva del gobierno".</p><p>Pero Goodman escribió: “aunque los problemas planteados no son insignificantes, no están debidamente ante esta Junta Electoral y, por lo tanto, no pueden ser tratados en este procedimiento”.</p><p>También dijo que Sigcho-López argumentó que los requisitos para los candidatos independientes eran desproporcionadamente altos —con insuficiente tiempo para reunir firmas. Goodman escribió que "es la legislatura la que debe abordar estos problemas...".</p><p>Ambos candidatos dicen que se sintieron inspirados a postularse como independientes cuando el representante Jesús “Chuy” García tomó la decisión de última hora de retirarse de la carrera y posicionar a su jefa de personal, Patty García, quien no está relacionada con el congresista, a ganar la primaria. El alcalde de Lyons, Chris Getty, también se postula como candidato independiente y sus peticiones no fueron impugnadas.</p><p>Sigcho-López calificó la recomendación como "un movimiento en su [Patty García y el representante García] juego contra los votantes".</p><p>Macías calificó el desafío a la petición de "privación de derechos".</p><p>"Byron y yo merecimos nuestros lugares en esta boleta con más de 34,000 firmas de la comunidad. Patty García sabe que no puede ganar en las urnas contra una competencia seria, así que sigue intentando eliminar sus opciones", destacó Macías. "Eliminar a tu competencia no es una estrategia de campaña, es privación de derechos".</p><p>Frente a los desafíos a sus candidaturas, Sigcho-Lopez y Macías se unieron para criticar el proceso estatal para candidatos independientes, que dicen que está diseñado para ayudar a los demócratas establecidos a mantenerse en el poder. Sigcho-López dijo que está dispuesto a llevar la lucha legal hasta la Corte Suprema de Illinois.</p><p>“Tengo más de 30,000 peticiones, mientras que la nominada demócrata y el republicano apenas tenían más de 1,000 peticiones entre ellos", dijo Sigcho-López. "Así que es vergonzoso e hipócrita que ellos impugnen esto por el número de firmas y vamos a seguir luchando. Y lo llevaremos ante la Corte Suprema de Illinois si es necesario".</p><p>Tanto Sigcho-López como Macías le comentaron al Chicago Sun-Times sobre el desafío de volver a visitar hogares para que los votantes firmaran declaraciones que probaran sus firmas, en un momento en que muchas comunidades dentro del distrito están afectadas por el Operativo Midway Blitz y la continua presencia del Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE).</p><p>"La gente tiene miedo de firmar declaraciones. La gente tiene miedo de abrir la puerta. La gente tiene miedo de salir a la calle", dijo Sigcho-López. "Es peor firmar un documento legal, especialmente para los representantes demócratas que deberían saber cuánto miedo hay en nuestra comunidad".</p><p>La campaña de Macías detalló tres difíciles casos de tener que volver a un hogar para que los firmantes firmaran una declaración, entre ellos el de una mujer que fue rociada con gas durante el Operativo Midway Blitz en Brighton Park.</p><p>La residente del vecindario de La Villita, Alicia Cíntora, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZsWdrDReB0/?igsh=MWptbnVzcGYzZDN3bQ%3D%3D" target="_blank" >grabó un video con</a> Macías sobre cómo se impugnó su firma.</p><p>"Firmé de buena fe y estoy realmente un poco enojada de que se cuestionara esto", contó Cintora.</p><p>Macías le dijo al Sun-Times a principios de julio que esperaba un desafío por parte del equipo de Patty García. Lo calificó de "asqueroso" que a dos candidatos latinos se les expulse de la boleta.</p><p>"Desde el principio ha quedado claro que ni Patty ni el representante García quieren que los votantes tengan voz en quién los representa, y están dispuestos a litigar esto a puerta cerrada en lugar de dejar que los votantes decidan en las urnas", dijo Macías. "Es realmente asqueroso ver que en el distrito más latino del estado, nuestro líder, que ha construido su carrera diciendo que está elevando y luchando por la comunidad latina, intenta activamente expulsar a candidatos latinos".</p><p>Patty García, la única demócrata en la boleta, ha recibido el apoyo de demócratas establecidos y de los sindicatos. El jueves, su campaña informó que recaudó $80,000 en el último trimestre de recaudación de fondos, lo que lleva el total de contribuciones a más de $350,000.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Man charged with carrying machete on CTA Green Line
entries.summary: <p>A man has been accused of carrying a machete and knife on a CTA Green Line train in Austin last weekend.</p><p>Ronald Reed, 31, was stopped by Cook County sheriff’s officers about 2:15 p.m. July 11 after officers noticed him holding an open beer can on the train near the Austin stop, the sheriff’s office said.</p><p>Officers searched Reed and found a machete with an 18-inch blade in a sling on his back, and a knife with a 5-inch serrated blade in a holster, police said.</p><p>Bodycamera footage shows a sheriff’s officer asking Reed at the Green Line station if he has anything on him before he searches him.</p><p>“I got a machete,” Reed says in the video, telling the officer it’s on his back.</p><p>Reed, of West Garfield Park, was arrested and charged with one count each of felony unlawful possession of a weapon and misdemeanor disorderly conduct.</p><p>A Cook County judge ordered him held in custody while he awaits trial.</p><p>Reed’s next court date was set for July 31.</p>

entries.title: White Sox not overthinking their surprising leap to contention: ‘Dumb enough to just go play hard’
entries.summary: <p>TORONTO — A slew of rookies playing out of their minds?</p><p>A trio of young infield sluggers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/18/munetaka-murakami-colson-montgomery-miguel-vargas-white-sox-home-runs" target="_blank" ><u>mashing</u></a> their way to national prominence?</p><p>A rotation with some questions on the back end, and a bullpen with even more glaring concerns?</p><p>It all just might be dumb enough to work for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a>.</p><p>“We joke about being just dumb enough to not know, and just being dumb enough to just go play hard, and let it take care of itself,” veteran outfielder Randal Grichuk told the Sun-Times.</p><p>He’s one of seven players in the Sox’ clubhouse with postseason experience, one of the few with more than a couple October games on his resume. Now Grichuk’s in a clubhouse full of players aching for their first taste of the playoffs, a prospect that few beyond 35th and Shields ever took seriously early in the spring.</p><p>“This room is really talented, and I think it's honestly more talented than the baseball world knows and would give us credit for, because we are so young and the teams out there, people out there, just don't really know,” Grichuk said. “It's been fun to be a part of it, helping them grow if I can.”</p><p>With the Sox coming out of the All-Star break in a first-place tie for the first time in five years — and opening their contending window <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/16/chicago-white-sox-chris-getz-will-venable-mlb-trade-deadline-blue-jays" target="_blank" ><u>well ahead of schedule</u></a> — that inexperience isn’t necessarily a bad thing.</p><p>“I think you could say it's a bit of an advantage,” said All-Star rookie Tristan Peters, the high-flying center fielder and former Savannah Banana who has made the Luis Robert Jr. era feel like a distant, melancholy memory.</p><p>“Somebody said this to me at the All-Star Game — they were just like, it just seems that we don't care. Not that we don't care, but we just play so loose,” Peters said. “It's a special team, and I think we just know how to have fun, and baseball is supposed to be fun.”</p><div class="Enhancement" division, and that came after we went from like 72-90 to 92-70. entries.title: Teen shot 7 times in Garfield Park
entries.summary: <p>A 17-year-old male was in critical condition after a shooting Friday afternoon in West Garfield Park, officials said.</p><p>The teen was sitting in a vehicle in the 3800 block of West Madison Street around 4:53 p.m., when he was approached by two unknown people, according to Chicago police. </p><p>The two fired multiple gunshots at the teen, police said, and he sustained seven gunshot wounds.</p><p>He then self-transported to Stroger Hospital, where he was listed in critical condition. </p><p>Detectives are investigating. <br></p>

entries.title: Pitching, pitching and more pitching on Jed Hoyer’s mind as championship-chasing Cubs approach trade deadline
entries.summary: <p>Welcome to mid July at Wrigley Field, where all eyes are on August and October.</p><p>The trade deadline is Aug. 3. It’s then that team president Jed Hoyer faces his last big chance to bolster a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> roster with championship-level expectations.</p><p>That means pitching, pitching and more pitching as the team <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/16/cubs-second-half-preview-brewers-nl-central-standings-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-craig-counsell-jed-hoyer-mlb-trade-deadline-alex-bregman" >emerges from the All-Star break in playoff position</a> but still hobbled from an avalanche of pitching injuries.</p><p>“We’re not ruling out any kind of position-player transaction,” Hoyer said Friday, “but the expectation is we will focus on our pitching staff.”</p><p>A team’s ability to compete in October is what drives decision-makers to be aggressive or conservative during trade season. An expanded postseason has meant more teams are, mathematically, able to consider themselves contenders.</p><p>The Cubs, though, are a contender with sky-high goals.</p><p>The question facing Hoyer is does he think this team is capable of achieving them? And if so, does that spark him and his front office to go big in August to try to assure a longer October run than last year?</p><p>“I try to not get overly emotional about it,” Hoyer said. “I try to stick to the numbers and make sure we’re doing things that make sense on paper. But I think our position-playing group is really, really good. … That’s a group that could win a lot of games in October.</p><p>“Obviously, the challenge for us has simply been pitching and pitching injuries.”</p><p>It’s a restating of the obvious from the Cubs’ baseball boss, who everyone knows will have pitching at the top of his shopping list.</p><p>In addition to a team ERA of 4.33 that ranked 21st in baseball coming into Friday, injuries hammered the staff during the first half. Lefty Matthew Boyd is back from his long layoff, and righties Jameson Taillon and Edward Cabrera will restock the starting rotation at some point.</p><p>But while some could suggest that improved health could be akin to a trade-deadline haul, Hoyer isn’t necessarily among them.</p><p>“You can’t have too much pitching. You never have enough,” he said. “The hope of guys coming back off the injured list, I don’t think that’s going to temper our need.</p><p>“I’d love to go, ‘Oh, we have too much,’ but I don’t see that ever really happening. I don’t think that would impact that considerably.”</p><p>So will it be a reliever here? A swingman there?</p><p>Or are we talking about the best starting pitcher available?</p><p>Hoyer going big might depend on how likely it is that the Cubs can be a playoff team with a first-round bye, waiting for an opponent to slog through a series just to make it to their doorstep. That’s what the Brewers were last year, when they ousted the Cubs in the NLDS.</p><p>“You have to go into the deadline, you have to think about it analytically, you have to think about: Getting a bye is effectively winning a series and weakening your opponent in the next series. That’s a really big deal,” Hoyer said. “If the odds say that you can do that, that’s a different equation than if not. You have to be aware of those things, and we certainly will be.”</p><p>Hoyer talked up his farm system, but he’s a year removed from balking at the high prospect cost of pitching and not making a move for a front-of-the-rotation arm last summer. However, that’s what he did in the offseason, shipping outfielder Owen Caissie to the Marlins for Cabrera.</p><p>Though Hoyer is always trying to balance the present and future, that move signaled a recognition of the Cubs’ ability to win now.</p><p>There’s a belief in the clubhouse that this team can do just that.</p><p>“If ownership and the [front office] decides, ‘We’re going to make a push, we’re going to do that,’ there’s a ton of belief of, ‘All right, this is the time to do it, time to get hot, time to play our best brand of baseball going into October,’” said righty reliever Phil Maton on the energizing effect of deadline deals, in general. “The expectations are to win a World Series here, and that’s exactly what we should be shooting for with the clubhouse that we have right now.”</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: At council hearing, Chicago police say they’ve implemented mayor’s order to target ICE — 6 months later
entries.summary: <p>City officials were summoned to a testy City Council committee hearing Friday to provide answers about the delayed implementation of Mayor Brandon Johnson’s order directing Chicago police to investigate potential crimes committed by federal immigration agents.</p><p>Members of the Committee on Immigrant and Refugee Rights spent about two hours peppering mayoral aides and police leaders with questions about Johnson’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/15/brandon-johnson-city-council-ice-immigration-midway-blitz" target="_blank" >“ICE on Notice”</a> executive order, asking what the decree has accomplished and what additional steps are needed to enforce it.</p><p>Police officials said the department had finalized internal procedures to implement the order, nearly five months after the mayor's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/01/31/brandon-johnson-investigate-ice-prosecution-executive-order-chicago" target="_blank" >30-day deadline</a>. However, they wouldn’t say why it took so long.</p><p>“We value CPD and want to believe that officers are indeed here to preserve and protect our communities. But it is long past time for accountability to the public,” said Ald. Andre Vasquez (40th), the committee chair.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-cf0000" name="image-cf0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3b9ffb5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fed%2F8c%2Fbd9bae4a4391819be4c33e99c5b7%2Fimmigrationhearing-260718-08.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9d0e1aa/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fed%2F8c%2Fbd9bae4a4391819be4c33e99c5b7%2Fimmigrationhearing-260718-08.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b390210/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fed%2F8c%2Fbd9bae4a4391819be4c33e99c5b7%2Fimmigrationhearing-260718-08.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Andre Vasquez (40th), chair of the Committee on Immigrant and Refugee Rights, speaks during a Friday committee hearing about the implementation of Mayor Brandon Johnson’s order cracking down on federal immigration agents.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Hours earlier, Johnson issued a news release urging people to come forward with allegations of wrongdoing stemming from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/09/08/trump-chicago-crime-pritzker-national-guard-ice-truth-social?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=090925%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=090925%20Morning%20Edition+CID_8198ca4c8936998efce45f5340df929e&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Trump%20launches%20long-promised%20Chicago%20deportation%20campaign&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" >Operation Midway Blitz</a>, the Trump administration’s pummeling deportation campaign last fall.</p><p>But the appeal did little to quell the frustrations of alderpersons and community members.</p><p>Committee members came prepared with a list of questions: How will the police department enforce the new policies? Has the entire department been notified of the changes? And who can file a police report if someone is detained by a federal agent?</p><p>Police officials said the department lacked a system for tracking complaints against federal agents. That means they had to establish new protocols for investigating those complaints, collecting evidence and identifying the federal agents who were involved.</p><p>Officers have been told to collect witness statements and submit reports, but the department won’t open criminal cases unless a victim or a victim’s relative comes forward.</p><p>“We have to work at the victim's wishes and what the victim wants us to do — if the victim wants to pursue the case report that was generated or doesn't,” said Patrick Kinney, commander in the Bureau of Detectives. </p><p>If a victim can’t file a report, a relative can come forward instead, officials said. That includes cases in which someone is detained by federal agents and family members can't locate them. Police can then open an investigation into an agent's conduct and the circumstances surrounding the arrest.</p><p>In Friday’s news release, Johnson’s office said the police department is reviewing a report issued in April by the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/04/30/pritzker-illinois-accountability-commission-operation-midway-blitz-trump-immigration" target="_blank" >Illinois Accountability Commission</a>, assembled by Gov. JB Pritzker to investigate abuses by Midway Blitz agents. Individuals named in the report — and others who “witnessed or experienced unlawful conduct” — were urged to contact the police department.</p><p>During last year’s enforcement blitz, city residents — and even cops — were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/13/tear-gas-federal-agents-immigration-enforcement-chicago-police-department-dan-oconnor" target="_blank" >tear-gassed</a>. Federal agents <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/14/ice-bovino-border-patrol-homeland-security-chicago-police-department" target="_blank" >caused traffic crashes</a> while making arrests. A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >woman was shot five times</a> on the city's Southwest Side, and an immigrant father was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/05/ice-midway-blitz-chicago-trump-silverio-villegas-gonzalez" target="_blank" >fatally shot</a> in suburban Franklin Park.</p><p>Police officials said they’re looking for eyewitnesses and evidence. They said they’ll use footage from police cameras and license plate readers to investigate reports of crimes.</p><p>And while police officials said some information could be released publicly, evidence and other investigative materials will remain confidential to preserve the integrity of any potential criminal prosecution.</p><p>"Our biggest concern is making sure that any evidence that is brought to us can be introduced into court," Kinney said. "Chain of custody is extremely important for us."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" a City Council committee hearing. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The hearing was held amid what local advocates have described as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/07/09/ice-arrests-increase-chicago-tactics-less-publicized-midway-blitz-back-yards-gage-brighton-park" target="_blank" >a surge in immigration enforcement</a>, and in the wake of two fatal shootings involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Texas and Maine.</p><p>No immigration agents have been charged with committing on-duty crimes in Cook County, despite loud calls for accountability. Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke has maintained that it’s up to police to investigate and refer cases to her office for charging.</p><p>That position was supported by Cook County Circuit Judge Erica Reddick, who rejected a request to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/special-prosecutor-midway-blitz-ice-trump-oneill-burke-cook-county" target="_blank" >appoint a special prosecutor</a> to investigate alleged crimes by federal immigration agents.</p>

entries.title: Illinois GOP trails badly in midterm cash
entries.summary: <p>The Illinois Republican Party filed its quarterly campaign finance report on the July 15 deadline. The party reported having just $223,000 in the bank. The next day, the party sent a letter to the Illinois State Board of Elections saying they were “reconciling” their records after a leadership change, and then noted that their actual end balance was $101,000 higher than it had reported the day before.</p><p>But that bit of found money was basically the end of the “good news” for the GOP last week.</p><p>Republicans no longer have a pet billionaire. Bruce Rauner and Ken Griffin have fled the state. The legions of wealthy business titans who once contributed and raised money have either retired to sunnier climes or passed away. Several prominent party members have publicly shunned labor unions and their hefty political war chests, although the state GOP legislative leaders have at least tried to rebuild ties to trade unions and even the Illinois Education Association. But the heavily gerrymandered legislative map, combined with the current political climate, means they’ll mostly receive scraps.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-570000" name="module-570000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>And, yes, the House Democrats are struggling this month with scandals, including a state representative who resigned under pressure and another who was indicted. I'm not trying to downplay that at all. But Democrats have the national political environment, the local infrastructure and tons of cash behind them. The Republicans have little to none of that.</p><p>The GOP's gubernatorial candidate, Darren Bailey, raised $1.3 million in the second quarter, which ended June 30. That sounds like a lot, but he spent almost all of that on direct mail fundraising costs. The huge expenditures do give him a prospect list for future fundraising, but he ended the quarter with a mere $128,000 in the bank. That was still a whole lot more than the rest of the statewide ticket.</p><p>Attorney General nominee Bob Fioretti, a perennial candidate, raised $31,000, spent $39,000 and had $28,000 on hand at the end of the quarter, along with almost $15,000 in recent debt. Secretary of State candidate Diane Harris raised $6,000, spent a bit over $4,000 and had a paltry $1,816.42 in the bank. Treasurer candidate Max Solomon, who ran as a write-in during the primary because the party failed to recruit anyone, raised less than $3,000, reported no spending and ended the quarter with less than $8,000. Comptroller candidate Bryan Drew raised $30,000 and received $47,000 in in-kind contributions from a company owned, ironically, by independent gubernatorial candidate Collin Corbett. Drew spent less than $3,000, ended with $54,000, and had $25,000 in debt from earlier this year.</p><p>Man, that’s just downright pathetic.</p><p>But I suppose it doesn’t really matter anyway unless we see a massive sea change in national opinion in the coming months or the federal government finds a way to not certify certain election results. Regardless of where individual candidates are at this moment, they'll have the money to compete. Unlike the Republicans, the Dems do have a pet billionaire (JB Pritzker), and I assume eventually for most of them, organized labor.</p><p>The Republican legislative leaders have tried to scrape and claw as much as they can, but they’re vastly outgunned. Senate Republican Leader John Curran raised just $75,000 in the second quarter. He spent $71,000 and reported having a bit more than $3 million in the bank. His caucus committee reported having $160,000 in the bank.</p><p>Leader Curran has three Republican-held districts to defend in the Chicago media market that have all trended Democratic in the last three cycles. Depending how bad things get, he could be defending a couple, two or three more.</p><p>The Senate Democrats have a ton of money to do whatever they want. Senate President Don Harmon has about $20 million in his personal campaign account and $1.7 million in his caucus account.</p><p>Over in the House, Republican Leader Tony McCombie has at least four Democratic-trending or swingy districts to defend and just $1.3 million in her personal campaign account and another $363,000 in her caucus account so far.</p><p>In contrast, House Speaker Chris Welch had $11.4 million in his personal account and $1.2 million in his caucus account. Like Harmon, he has more than enough money already, but more is never enough when there’s so much out there, so those numbers will likely rise by November.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-870000" name="module-870000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: West Loop's Fairlife pauses U.S. production after cyberattack
entries.summary: <p>Chicago-based dairy company Fairlife paused U.S. production after its systems were breached in a ransomware attack.</p><p>Fairlife, maker of ultra-filtered milk and Core Power protein shakes, is a subsidiary of the Coca-Cola Co.</p><p>The company said Thursday that the breach included parts of Fairlife’s production systems, but product quality and safety were not affected. However, “the full scope, nature and impacts of the incident are not yet known,” according to its news release. Fairlife’s production in Canada is unaffected.</p><p>The company is investigating and assessing the incident with the help of cybersecurity experts and has notified law enforcement. It’s working to restore systems and operations.</p><p>There was no update as of Friday afternoon, a Coca-Cola spokesperson said.</p><p>Fairlife was founded in 2012 and bought by Coca-Cola in 2020. It’s headquartered in the West Loop and has facilities in Michigan, Arizona, New York and New Mexico.</p><p>Fairlife’s annual retail sales exceed $3 billion, according to its website.</p><p>Companies and Chicago-area institutions have faced a number of cyberattacks.</p><p>In June, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/08/evanston-township-high-school-cancel-summer-classes-until-wednesday-over-weekend-cyberattack" >Evanston Township High School</a> was hit with a ransomware attack that forced it to temporarily cancel summer classes, sports camps and other on-campus activities.</p><p>In May, a cyberattack on the online learning platform <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/05/08/university-of-illinois-finals-postponed-canvas-schools-cyberattack-hacked" >Canvas</a> caused disruptions at many Illinois colleges and schools. Canvas’ temporary shutdown forced the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign to postpone some exams and assignments.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/05/08/university-of-illinois-finals-postponed-canvas-schools-cyberattack-hacked" >Canvas hack leads U. of I. to postpone finals, schools scramble without popular learning tool</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/13/chicago-digitalmint-hack-ransomware-crime-angelo-martino-marc-grens" >Chicago cybersecurity firm employee brokered $75M in ransom after orchestrating hacks, feds say</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
